subject: radiology
title: Golden S Sign and Westermark Sign on Chest Films

steps.title: Golden S from a central tumour
steps.tx: **Golden S sign** appears when a central right upper lobe tumour blocks the bronchus and the lobe collapses around the mass. The horizontal fissure droops at its lateral end under the collapsed lobe weight but bulges downward near the hilum where tumour bulk props it up, tracing a reverse S curve. That convex medial bulge separates tumour collapse from simple benign collapse, whose fissure stays concave throughout.

steps.title: Right upper lobe collapse basics
steps.tx: **Right upper lobe collapse** pulls the horizontal fissure upward and the trachea rightward as volume leaves the lobe. Without tumour, the fissure bows smoothly upward in one concave arc and the opacity hugs the mediastinum. Children collapse this lobe around aspirated foreign bodies and mucus plugs in asthma, while adults over forty with a smoking history collapse it around bronchogenic carcinoma until proven otherwise.

steps.title: Westermark sign in embolism
steps.tx: **Westermark sign** is a focal region of hyperlucency where a pulmonary embolus has cut arterial flow and emptied the vessels beyond it. The affected segment looks washed out beside normally perfused lung, with vessels that stop abruptly at the clot. Sensitivity is low because most emboli are too small or too central to empty a visible territory, so a normal looking film never excludes pulmonary embolism.

steps.title: Hampton hump and Palla sign
steps.tx: **Hampton hump** is the dome shaped pleural based opacity of pulmonary infarction, its base on the pleura and its rounded apex pointing at the hilum. Palla sign instead shows an enlarged right pulmonary artery with a sausage shape from clot distending it. Both signs support embolism on a plain film, but CT pulmonary angiography remains the test that confirms clot, maps its burden and excludes mimics.

steps.title: Oligaemia versus hyperinflation
steps.tx: **Focal oligaemia** from embolism keeps normal lung volume in the pale territory, separating it from air trapping where the pale side expands and flattens its diaphragm. A unilateral hyperlucent lung in a child more often means an inhaled foreign body with check valve air trapping, best shown by an expiratory film where the pale side stays inflated. Embolism patients are usually breathless adults with pleuritic pain or haemoptysis instead.

steps.title: Golden S demands tissue diagnosis
steps.tx: **Bronchoscopy** follows a Golden S film because imaging alone cannot grade or type the tumour causing collapse. The scope finds most central lesions directly, since nearly nine in ten bronchogenic carcinomas causing this sign sit within a main or lobar bronchus. Biopsy type then drives staging CT and treatment, while the collapsed lobe may re expand after stenting or radiotherapy relieves the block.

steps.title: Silhouette loss joins the Golden S
steps.tx: **Mediastinal silhouette** loss often accompanies right upper lobe tumour collapse because the opaque lobe touches the upper mediastinum and ascending aorta. The upper right mediastinal border vanishes while the heart border lower down stays crisp. Combining border loss with the fissure S curve doubles confidence that the opacity is right upper lobe and central in origin before any cross sectional study is booked.

steps.title: Embolism signs never rule out
steps.tx: **Plain film signs** of pulmonary embolism, Westermark, Hampton hump and Palla together, still miss most cases because small peripheral clots change nothing visible. A high clinical probability with a clear film proceeds straight to CT pulmonary angiography or a ventilation perfusion study when contrast is barred. D dimer only helps when probability is low or intermediate, where a negative result safely avoids imaging.
